name: Communication between containers

home_this_is: This is the home page of the Docker container communication learning app.
home_p_1: The application contains tasks to demonstrate all available types of Docker networks. Each task contains in the first section the theoretical part of the given Docker network. In the second section, a practical task is specified. In the third section there is a visualization canvas, where the current state of Docker containers, networks and network elements relevant to the given task is reflected.
home_p_2: To complete the task, it is necessary to verify the correctness of the task using the button located on the task visualization screen.
home_p_3: Docker is an open-source platform for containerizing applications to simplify their development and deployment. Docker creates so-called containers. These containers contain applications, all the necessary dependencies, libraries, and tools to run these applications. Containers are isolated from the outside environment, just like virtual machines. Unlike virtual machines, Docker containers do not create their own operating system, but run on the same operating system as their host device. The main advantage of this difference is that Docker containers are less burdensome for the system and faster to start. Containers are easily portable, since all the dependencies needed to run a containerized application are predefined in the container image.
home_p_4: Working with Docker is facilitated by two basic objects - containers and images. A Docker image is a template with a set of instructions according to which a Docker container is to be created. A container is an instance of a Docker image that we can work with, stop, delete, modify. Docker uses a client-server architecture. There are three components behind the functioning of Docker: Docker client, Docker daemon, Docker registry. The Docker client is the layer through which the user interacts with Docker, it can be via a terminal, Docker desktop, which is a graphical interface of Docker, or another external interface. The Docker client communicates with the Docker daemon via a REST API. The task of the Docker daemon is to receive signals from the client and create or modify Docker containers, images, networks according to them. Both the client and the daemon can run on one host device. The daemon's job is to manage the registry of images on the host machine, but it also communicates with an online Docker registry, also called Dockerhub, where it can upload or download Docker images. This registry is used to upload Docker images that are made available to the public or a specific group of people.
home_p_5: Docker achieves virtualization of the environment using cgroups and namespaces. The task of cgroups is to limit and control system resources for groups of processes such as RAM, CPU. They have a tree structure, where the root of the structure is the root itself and the children are groups of processes that share the same resources. The root cgroup contains all processes of the system. There are several types of cgroups and each process is represented in each type of cgroup. For example, there are memory cgroups that allocate and limit a specific portion of memory for a group of processes. When we decide to allocate a certain amount of memory for a specific group of processes, this information passes through the root of the cgroup structure, which ensures that no other group uses this portion of memory. On the other hand, namespaces limit what a group of processes can see. Namespaces are also represented by a tree structure. Again, there are multiple namespaces and each process is located in each type of namespace. We know the pid namespace, which ensures that processes within a single namespace can only see other processes in the same namespace, so each Docker container only sees its own processes, as if it were the only device in the system. The network namespace allows each container to grant and isolate its own network resources. User namespaces are used to separate the powers of the same users across namespaces. So, one system user is mapped to a different identifier in the host device namespace than in the container environment.
defaultBridge_p1: The default bridge network is pre-created after Docker is installed and is an isolated, internal network that allows containers located on this network to communicate within a single host device. Within Docker networks, it is called bridge and is created according to the bridge driver. Internally, the Docker bridge is actually a bridge network component within the Linux ecosystem and its network heap under the name docker0, which we can verify with the command to list network interfaces on the host computer running Docker. It is the default because after creating any Docker container without specifying its network, this container is connected to this bridge network.
defaultBridge_p2: The default Docker bridge network gets its own subnet and gateway. From this IP range, all containers created on this network then get their own IP address. The built-in IPAM service is used to assign IP addresses. An internal Docker library that is responsible for selecting a free address range for the default bridge network. This setting is configurable by editing the daemon.json configuration file. If we have not explicitly defined which range we want to use, the library looks for a free range in the default ranges, namely 172.x.x.x/16, then 192.168.x.x/16 or 10.x.x.x/8.
defaultBridge_p3: The default bridge network does not allow the user to dynamically modify its settings, in case of modification, a restart of the Docker service is required. The modifiable settings for the default bridge network are limited, and in case we need to customize and modify the bridge network settings, it is better to create a user-defined bridge network. The Docker bridge driver sets the rules for the host machine, where containers connected to other bridge networks do not have access to communicate with each other. For communication, egress is enabled by default, so the container is able to communicate with the outside world, we are able to query a page on the Internet. However, ingress, or communication between the outside world and the container, is disabled. Docker allows the container to communicate with the outside network by revealing the port. It is necessary to map the container port with a free port on the host machine, thus enabling ingress communication, such mapping can be defined when creating the container. The default bridge network does not include a DNS mechanism for containers connected to it; we can only query the container using its IP address.
defaultBridge_p4: Once a container is connected to the bridge network, it is given a network interface. This container network interface is connected to a virtual Ethernet pair located in the host machine space, and a Linux bridge is connected to the other side of the virtual Ethernet pair, from which the network is then redirected to the outside world using NAT technology.

defaultBridge_task_step3: Validate access to containers and their communication.
defaultBridge_task_instruction: To test egress communication, you can use the ping command. Also test container-to-container communication using IP address and container name. Ingress can be verified by accessing port 80 where the nginx server is running.
bridge_overview_p1: A user-defined bridge network is created by the user and, like the default bridge network, is created using the bridge driver. In the Linux ecosystem, it is again a Linux bridge, which is named based on the Docker bridge network ID and the prefix br-.
bridge_overview_p2: It allows easier network modification without restarting Docker. When creating the network, we can define a custom subnet from which all connected containers will get their own IP address.
bridge_overview_p3: Unlike the default bridge network, the user-defined bridge network includes a DNS mechanism that enables mapping of IP addresses by container name. This allows container communication using container names.
bridge_overview_p4: The image shows a demonstration of a user-defined bridge network named my-bridge and also the default Docker bridge network. The second row shows the name of the Linux bridge. If necessary, a container can be connected to multiple networks at once, and it will receive a new network interface.

host_overview_description: The host network removes any isolation between the host and containers, meaning containers have direct access to the host's network environment and use its network parameters. As a result, a container using the host network has the same IP address as the host machine. The advantage of using the host network is improved performance of the application running in the container, meaning that packet transmission and reception are faster because the container is directly connected to the host's network interface, without additional networking technologies in between such as NAT, bridge, or VXLAN tunnel. The disadvantage is that the container is directly exposed to the outside world, which poses a higher security risk. Anyone with access to the host machine also has access to the container, meaning ingress is allowed—unlike in the bridge network, where you need to explicitly expose the desired port. Another disadvantage is that the port used by the container on the host network cannot be used by another application, causing limitations when running multiple Docker containers. In the image, we can see a host computer running an SSH service on port 22 and an nginx Docker container connected to the Docker host network on port 80.

ipvlan_overview_paragraph_1: Docker provides the IPVLAN networking mode via the ipvlan driver. IPVLAN allows containers to connect directly to the host’s physical network using virtual sub-interfaces, which—unlike MACVLAN—share the same MAC address. This MAC address is identical to the MAC address of the parent network interface. IPVLAN networks operate on both Layer 2 and Layer 3, whereas MACVLAN networks only operate on Layer 2. Unlike MACVLAN, IPVLAN does not require promiscuous mode, improving security. Another advantage is support for wireless networking, which MACVLAN does not support.

ipvlan_task_step_2: Create 2 BusyBox Docker containers connected to the Docker IPVLAN network, named busybox-1 and busybox-2.
ipvlan_task_step_3: Validate access to the containers and their communication.
ipvlan_task_description: To test egress communication, you can use the ping command. Also test inter-container communication using both IP address and container name. Ingress can be verified by accessing port 80 where the nginx server is located. Compare the differences between nginx containers on IPVLAN and MACVLAN networks.
macvlan_overview_paragraph_1: For the MACVLAN network, Docker provides a driver called MACVLAN. Using this driver, we can create a Docker MACVLAN network in bridge mode and use it for our containers. The MACVLAN network allows assigning each container a unique MAC address, making them appear as separate devices on the local network. Containers connected to the MACVLAN network are directly attached to the physical network. It is necessary to define a parent network interface, which is used by the local device to communicate with the outside world. A subnet and local gateway must also be defined. With this configuration, MACVLAN is capable of assigning containers IP addresses from the local network. This network is useful when we want the container to connect directly to an external network without additional layers like bridge, NAT, or VXLAN technologies used in bridge and overlay Docker networks. The advantages include faster communication due to fewer intermediaries and unique identification using IP and MAC addresses. Unlike the host network, we can run multiple containers on the same host using the same port without conflicts. However, MACVLAN also brings security concerns, as containers are directly exposed to the local network and require specific security configurations.
macvlan_overview_paragraph_2: A key configuration for MACVLAN to function properly is enabling promiscuous mode on the parent network interface. This mode allows a physical interface to have multiple MAC addresses. This setting is needed so the host can receive packets addressed to the containers' MAC addresses.
macvlan_overview_paragraph_3: The image demonstrates a Docker MACVLAN network using the host's eth0 interface. IP addresses are assigned to the containers from the local subnet, and each container gets a unique MAC address.

none_overview_description: None means the container network is completely disabled; the container is isolated from all other containers and the host machine. The container cannot communicate with any other entity and does not allow ingress communication. The only network interface inside the container is the loopback interface.

overlay_overview_intro_1: So far, we have only introduced options for connecting containers within a single host machine. In real production environments, it is also essential to enable communication and linking containers across multiple host machines running Docker. This is where overlay networks come in. To create a Docker overlay network, we must set up a Docker Swarm on the main host machine acting as a manager and connect all other hosts as workers to this Swarm. Docker Swarm manages and synchronizes information about each host and its network details. This is crucial for communication as it provides the overlay network with information about the target Docker container to which packets should be sent.
overlay_overview_intro_2: However, communication within an overlay network is complex because the data sent through the network is multi-layer encapsulated. The communication uses VXLAN technology. Data segments sent by containers via the overlay network receive an IP header with the sender's and receiver's IP addresses. The IP packet is then encapsulated in an Ethernet frame. To transport the packet across the physical network, the frame is wrapped in a VXLAN header containing a 24-bit network identifier (VNI). The data is then packaged in a UDP datagram and further gets an IP header with the IP address of the host machine running the sending Docker container and the IP address of the destination host machine. The packet is again wrapped in an Ethernet frame with MAC addresses and sent through the physical network to the destination host, where it is unpacked and delivered to the Docker container.
overlay_overview_intro_3: Upon creating the Docker overlay network via Docker Swarm, the Docker engine automatically creates a VXLAN tunnel and Linux bridge in a network namespace named after the overlay network’s ID. These network components are isolated from the host network namespace. A virtual ethernet pair connects the Docker container's interface to the Linux bridge in the namespace. Data from the bridge is passed to the VXLAN tunnel.
overlay_overview_intro_4: The Docker Swarm manager ensures the creation of a data store holding information about all containers, their VTEPs, and VNIs within the overlay network. It synchronizes this data among all workers. When a new device joins the network, all others are notified, and their stores are updated.
overlay_overview_intro_5: When using Docker Swarm, the Docker engine also automatically creates a Docker bridge network called docker_gwbridge in the host's namespace. This bridge connects to another network interface inside Docker containers, acting as an egress gateway, allowing data to exit containers to the outside world. Communication between containers on this network is disabled.
